【51】**Frank myopathy is suggested both clinically， with distally pronounced muscle wasting， and on CT scanning of leg muscles， which reveals a selective pattern of fatty change. This is in contrast to McLeod syndrome， in which findings tend to be symmetrical 删除1:<u>(Ishikawa et al.， 2000)</u>. However， neurogenic changes are more commonly detected on electromyography.**

【52】**Diagnostic Tests**

【53】Genetic sequencing of the VPS13A gene with proof of mutation is the diagnostic gold standard 删除1:<u>(Dobson-Stone et al.， 2002)</u>. The diagnosis of the disease is clear if one homozygous or two heterozygous mutations are found on both alleles of the gene. This test has recently become commercially available . Genetic analysis is difficult due to the large size of the VPS13A gene and the fact that mutations are distributed among all introns and exons. In a few patients， a mutation is found only on one allele. This is likely due to technical issues， for example， methodology which does not detect large dele-tions， rather than to dominant transmission， which remains controversial 删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Bader et al.， 2009； Ishida et al.， 2009； Saiki et al.， 2003)</u></u>.

【54】Detection of the protein product of VPS13A (chorein) is a simpler and cheaper test than genetic analysis. Absent or markedly reduced chorein from blood samples (erythrocyte membrane preparations) is suggestive of ChAc 删除1:<u>(Dobson-Stone et al.， 2004)</u>. The chorein Western blot is available free of charge .

【55】**Chronically increased CK values of more than 500 U/l are seen in two-thirds of ChAc patients and， in addition to elevated liver enzymes， may be more useful in indicating the diagnosis than the presence of acanthocytes.**

【56】**THERAPY**

【57】**Physical Therapy，Medical Aids， and Appliances**

【58】There is as yet no curative treatment for ChAc. Mechanical protective dev

【0】kills. The Calculation subtest evaluates written calculation and mathematics skills. from basic addition and subtraction to algebra at the intermediate level and inte-gral calculus at the highest level. Information from this measure gives the clinician a sense of the client's mathematics proficiency. The Applied Problems subtest shows how well the client can apply his or her skills to solving mathematic problems. For some， this can be the primary deficit area， even with strong calculational skills. Individuals with diffi-culties on this subtest often have impairments in executive functioning and conceptual thinking， which limit their ability to apply their knowl-edge to problem solving. Finally， the Quantitative Concepts subtest pro-vides information on mathematical knowledge (i.e.， meanings of operations， signs， and symbols).**

【1】**When scores on mathematics measures are far below expectations， based on the client's intellectual potential， recommendations can be made for exemption from math requirements and for pursuit of a major that does not place demands on advanced mathematics skills. There also is evidence thal extended time can improve test scores in those with mathematics disabilities 删除1:<u>(Alster， 1997)</u>. If underlying deficits in other cognitive skills are contributing to problems in mathematics， interventions can be directed toward compensating for weaknesses.**

【2】**Nonverbal Learning Disability**

【3】**The syndrome of nonverbal or “right hemisphere”learning disabilities(NLD) has been described since the early 1970s 删除1:<u>(Semrud-Clikeman &Hynd， 1990)</u>. Key features that have been reported include average to well above average verbal intellectual skills， but deficits in social percep tion that affect judgments needed to succeed in everyday life. Additional difficulties have been reported in left-right orientation， reading maps or following directions， and mathematics 删除1:<u>(Semrud-Clikeman & Hynd，1990)</u>.**

【4】**Rourke (1995a) has described and researched nonverbal learning disabilities in some depth， although primarily as a disorder of children and adolescents. He has outlined the strengths and weaknesses associat-ed with the syndrome. According to Rourke (1995a)， notable strengths are observed in auditory perception， speech and language， smgle-word reading， spelling， attention to auditory verbal information. rote verbal memory， and simple motor skills. In contrast， deficits occur in tactile perception， visuospatial perceptual skills， complex psychomotor skills， concept formation， novel problem solving， hypothesis testing， use of feedback， pragmatic use of language， reading comprehension， arith-metic， and mathematic reasoning. Difficulties with social competence， adapting to new situations， and emotional disturbance are very com-mon and have a profound impact on everyday functioning. In many individuals， symptoms of anxiety and depression become worse over the years. Rourke (1995b) and colleagues have applied the syndrome of nonverbal learning disabilities to help understand problems observed in diseases with neurological effects， such as Williams syndroine； treat-ments with neurological side effects， such as radiation for cancer； and acquired neurological disorders， such as traumatic brain injury. Within this chapter， however， nonverbal learning disability is used to refer to a dis order that is developmental and does not have a clear neurological cause.**

**In my experience with adults， most， although not all， of the charac teristics described by Rourke (1995a) apply. Many of these clients report problems with attention and organization. Some report a past diagnosis of ADHD or seek assessinent because they believe they have ADHD. Yet， their social and psychiatric problems are usually more extreme and their cognitive problems are somewhat different from Lhose with ADHD. Although they have problems with attention and executive functions， clients with NLD have more pervasive problems in visuospatial and motor skills， in comparison to clients with ADHD. Some have struggled|删除0换行|in school since childhood， while others have successfully completed advanced degrees. For example， I saw a physician who had difficulty holding a job as a pathologist because of slowness and odd behavior despite board certification and good pathology skills. Most， however， have a history of problems maintaining erployment because they work very slowly and have difficulty with social relations.**

【6】**When seen for evaluation， these adults have obvious problems with social skills. This is evident during the initial interview， in which they appear awkward and anxious. Their prosody may be limited or may be incongruent with verbal content， and their speaking rate or volume may be poorly modulated. They may have difficulty with interpersonal dis-tance and with reading the clinician's nonverbal communication. These clients report a history of poor social relations； usually they have few or no friends and report few or no intimate relationships. Their problems are longstanding and date to childhood. They report having been shy withdrawn， and frequently tormented or teased by others as children. As adults， they report being extremely anxious in social situations， as well as when demands are placed on complex cognitive skills. Many also report being depressed. Asperger's syndrome is an extreme form of this disorder.**

【7】**Cognitively， the first prominent finding is a Verbal IQ that far exceeds Performance IQ. In some individuals， I have seen a phenomenal Verbal IQ of 140 or higher， with a Performance IQ of 100 to 110. In others， the Verbal IQ， although strong， is lower (e.g.， 120)， with a Performance IQ that is comparably weaker (c.g.80 to 90). In both cases， the clinical presentation and reports of life failures are similar. On testing， these individuals have problems with focused and sustained attention， process-ing speed， executive functioning， and visuospatial skills. Their problems on visuospatial perceptual and constructional tasks resemble those of patients with documented right-hemisphere pathology. For example， they may misperceive line drawings on the Boston Naming Test； may struggle to complete measures of visuospatial perceptual skills， such as those of Benton； and may break configuration or otherwise have problems organizing and planning their approacl when copying block designs on the WAIS-III or when copying drawings， such as the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure. Problems with fine motor speed and dexterity are fre-quent， often with relatively poorer performnance on the left. Handwriting typically is difficult to read.**

**Interestingly， I have fourid that mathematics skills are not always impaired in these individuals. One individual I tested achieved a score of 120 on a measure of written calculation， although he worked|删除0换行|extremely slowly. Yet， he could not work at a cash register because of slowness and anxiety. A second， the physician mentioned above， excelled in math， reporting that he enjoyed "developing equations”as a hobby. Indeed， there is some clinical lore suggesting that those who enjoy engineering， computers， and other technical fields may show a higher prevalence of NLD because some jobs in these fields require lit-tle social interaction. Yet， these jobs place strong demands on mathe-matics skills.**

【9】**I also have encountered individuals who show the same Verbal-Performance IQ discrepancy， but show less extreme cognitive problems and none of the psychosocial difficulties. These individuals are typically highly verbal， excelling in language skills and in analytical tasks that emphasize language. Yet they have attentional difficulties， process infor-mation slowly， organize poorly， and do not manage their time wel. Their mathematics skills may be weak. Because of their exceptionally strong verbal skills they tend to be introspective people who ruminate obsessively about intellectual or emotional issues. As a result， despite good social skills， they are anxious and can doubt their own abilities. However， the anxiety disorder does not appear to be primary； rather， it seems to be part of their cognitive processing style and their LD. These individuals do not show the full NLD syndrome； their social relation-ships are usually good， their motor skills can be strong， and some excel in athletics.**

【10】**Accommodations for the attentional and organizational problems associated with NLD include extended time on testing， a note-taker， and exemption from mathematics courses if mathematics is a significant weakness. These individuals are likely to do best in a major that empha-sizes verbal skills and minimizes demands on interpersonal skills. Some， despite weak visuospatial skills， do well in the computer field， in which they can work independently and away from others. However， speed can be a problem for them. Frequently， however， their problems with social skills are more limiting than their cognitive problems and， as noted， psy-chiatric co-morbidity is high. Therefore， structured individual and group psychotherapy， with an emphasis on social skill development and application of cognitive-behavioral strategies， can be an important com-ponent of treatment.**

【11】**Attention and Executive Functioning Disorders**

**Although impairments in attention and executive functioning are most common in individuals with ADHD， there are some adults wlto do|删除0换行|not meet behavioral criteria for the standard forms of ADHD (i.e.， predominantly inattentive， predominantly hyperactive/impulsive，com-bined) yet show impairment in attention and executive functioning on testing and in everyday life. They can be characterized as having an LD that affects attention and/or executive functioning， although they may be considered as falling into the diagnostic category of ADHD， not otherwise specified.**

【13】**These clients report that they cannot compleie their schoolwork or tasks assigned at work in the allotted time， stating they work longer and harder than peers to achieve similar outcomes. In school， completing tests in the allotted time is especially difficult. They also report prob-lems with attention. On neuropsychological testing， they perform slow-ly but accurately on measures of focused and sustained attention. Because of their slowness， their Performance IQ is low， and they have timed (or even extended time) scores on the NDRT that are below expectations.Most of these individuals show no evidence of depression or anxiety that can explain their slowness. Although some may meet cri-teria for diagnosis of ADHD， primarily inattentive type， many do not. Despite Barkley’s (1998) report that individuals with the inattentive form of ADHD do not benefit from psychostimulant treatment， in my experience many of these individuals， including those who are slow on ineasures of focused and sustained attention but do not meetADHD cri-teria at all， cart benefit from medication. It is possible that those who respond well to psychostimulants may have met criteria for hyperactivity as children but no longer do so as adults because of the decrease in hyperactivity with age 删除1:<u>(Barkley，1998)</u>.**

【14】**Other individuals show a purer executive-functioning disorder. They report everyday problems with time management and organization， complaining that they start many tasks but do not finish them. Initiation can be a problem， with the result of procrastination， handing in assign-ments late， or completing projects beyond deadlines. On testing， they have problems with flexibility of thinking， planning， and organization. They are impulsive， which affects their performance on administered measures. Learning and memory skills are weak. Yet they do not meet criteria for diagnosis of ADHD. I rarely recommend a medication evalu-ation for these individuals unless they show evidence of imnpairment in attention.**

**For these clients， accommodations and compensatory strategies rec-ommended for those with ADHD can be helpful. These include extra time on testing， individual testing， and a note-taker， especially if organi-zation is a problem. Those with more problems with and impairment in|删除0换行|executive functioning can benefit from the structure and behavioral strategies that are helpful for those with ADHD. Some may benefit from coaching and the additional structure that it provides.**

【16】**Learning and Memnory Disorders**

【17】**Most adults with LDs have associated problems with learning and mem~ory. Yet I have evaluated individuals with a purer disorder of learning and memory. Although less common than the LDs discussed， individu-als occasionally present with this type of problem. To my knowledge， this is not an LD that has been documented in the literature on chil-dren or adults. For adults referred for neuropsychological evaluation， the cause of a learning and memory difficulty problem is usually neuro-logical： TBI， seizure disorder， multiple sclerosis， or， later in life， demen-tia. Yet， these individuals report no history of a neurological disorder that could account for their problems with learning and memory. In their presentation， they report that deliberate learning of new informa-tion is very difficult. If they are in school， they report having to study much harder than their peers. Many attempt to learn information by rote， which， given the primary problem with learning and memory makes studying even harder. They cannot “cram" for tests the night before， because of the additional time they need to learn new informa-tion. Taking tests， both classroom and standardized， is very difficult； poor test performance and associated poor grades may be their primary complaint when seeking evaluation. Learning a foreign language can be very hard because of demands on rote learning. Most also are forgetful in everyday activities and may even show some unawareness of the extent of their everyday memory problems. A parent with whom the person lives may be the one who reports the difficulty.**

【18】**On testing， these individuals show poor initial learning of new infor-mation， even with repetition. Retention may be poor， and recognition may be no better than recall. Yet， these individuals show normal intel lectual skills， normal academic test performance， and no other specific cognitive weaknesses that could explain their difficulty.**

【19】**These individuals benefit from development of compensatory strate~gies and mnemonic methods to help them learn and retain material more effectively. They must learn to use the organization of the infor-mation to help them learn it more effectively. Having extended time on testing can sometimes help by giving them additional time to retrieve learned information fron memory. I also refer these individuals for a neurological evaluation to be sure there is not an undiagnosed condi-tion that could explain the problem.**

【20】**Self-Esteem and Emotional Issues**

【21】**Including objective personality measures， such as the MMPI-2， is impor-tant in order to rule out a psychiatric disorder that can explain learning problems. It is also important to evaluate psychiatric disorders that can be co-morbid with ALD， but not a primary explanation. Because long-standing problems with self-esteem and self-confidence are common in ALD， psychological testing can also help identify issues that can be addressed through psychotherapy when these problems are secondary to the LD. Many adults with LDs have gone through life feeling that they are stupid or that they are failures. Often criticized harshly for their slowness to learn in their early years of school， they internalized the criticism over the years， defining themselves by others' opinions rather than by objective evidence of their own success. Learning-disabled adults can be their own worst critics， focusing on the negative rather than the positive.**

【22】**Adults who show clear evidence of a learning disability， but have not been diagnosed in the past， can often benefit from psychotherapy 删除1:<u>(Vogel& Forness， 1992)</u>. Short-term psychotherapy can help them accept the diagnosis， which many had come to suspect， and can help thein learn to be less hard on themselves for their shortcomings. A professional who specializes in psychotherapy with learning-disabled adults can help clients identify and learn to appreciate their unique talents and strengths， further improving their often abysmal and inaccurate self-perceptiori. Educational and career counseling can be part of the process；learning"disabled adults can learn about academic or career directions that will emphasize their strengths anid place fewer demands on their weaknesses. Directive therapists may even help their clients learn how to compen-sate for their problems in everyday functioning. However， psychothera-pists must be familiar with the effects of an LD on cognitive processing modifying traditional verbal therapy as necessary. For those with a ver-bal LD or attentional probleis， this can include breaking information into smnall pieces， repeating information， and having the client para~phrase what was said. For those with a nonverbal LD， this may mean relying more on what is said and less on the nonverbal component of how it is said； commnunicating nonverbal information may have to be made explicitly verbal.**

**Self-esteem issues also have implications for the assessment process. Because adults with LDs associate testing with failure， they can be very anxious and apprehensive about going through a long battery of tests， the results of which may show them even more negative things about|删除0换行|themselves. For this reason， the clinician must make every effort to make the evaluation experience a positive one. Sometimes， this means giving more feedback and encouragement than neuropsychologists typ-ically do. This may also mean testing limits to allow clients to complete a task successfully， even when it requires more testing time. The time spent will be well rewarded， since the result will be a better indicator of the client's strengths and weaknesses. Moreover， the client will come away with a positive view of the process and will be more likely to follow up on recommendations made.**

【24】**Differential Diagnosis**

【25】**Ruling out other neurological， psychiatric， or medical disorders that can catse cognitive disturbance is the final step of assessment. When doing so， keep in mind that ALDs are developmentul disorders and require exclusion of acquired neurological disorders of cognition， from child-hood or adulthood， as the primary cause of learning problems. Therefore， as noted， history is critical， particularly because of overlap in the cognir live profiles of other disorders and LDs. That is， a diagnosis of LD can-not be made solely on the basis of test results but must be made in the context of what is known about the individual. ALDs also are frequent in individuals with certain disorders including TBI， alcoholism， and substance abuse. This is because individuals with LDs or other develop-mental disorders， such as ADHD， tend to be risk takers and impulsive. These behaviors increase their risk for brain injury and the likelihood of substance abuse. Alcohol or substance abuse can also begin because of psychological issues associated with LDs. Finally， ALD can coexist with ADHD， making an assessment of ADHD an important part of the evaluation. In sum， diffcrential diagnosis is accomplished by taking a careful history and by considering the pattern of neuropsychological performance in the context of the client's history.**

【4】**GENERAL STRATEGY**

【5】**History**

【6】Determine the amount of weight gain and specify over what period oftime.

【7】Determine what constitutes the patient's diet； fol-low with a diet diary.

【8】Determine whether the patient is taking any med-ications that may increase fluid retention or appetite.

【9】Determine the patient’s family history with regard to obesity and diabetes.

【10】Determine whether the patient has recently stopped smoking.

【11】Determine any changes in exercise levels.

【12】Determine whether the patient is under stress and uses food for relaxation or reward.

【13】Determine whether the patient has any symptoms of hypoglycemia (insulinoma； rare).

【14】**Examination**

【15】Weigh and measure height of the patient.

【16】**Determine the BMI.**

【17】Determine the patient's percentage of body fat with skin calipers or an impedance device (referral for wa-ter immersion method is less practical， but most accurate).

【18】Examine the patient for signs of fluid retention in abdomen and legs.

【19】Examine the patient for congestive heart failure if suspected from history (difficulty breathing while lying recumbent) and obtain a chest radiograph.

【20】Perform laboratory evaluation if the patient has historical and/or physical signs of diabetes，Cushing's lisease， or liypothyroidism.

【21】**Management**

【26】#### Introduction

【27】Dementia is defined as the development of cognitive deficits such that a patient is unable to perform his or her usual activities and the cognitive impairment is not due to an acute confusional state. Persons with life-long cognitive impairment do not meet this definition because they never were able to function at a higher level. Some, but not all, definitions of dementia require memory impairment as part of the syndrome. Because Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent cause of dementia in the industrialized world, the notion of “gradual progression” is sometimes considered part of the definition, but clearly dementia can be sudden in onset. For example, a patient who suffers a traumatic brain contusion will at first be obtunded or in coma, but after awakening and when alert, might meet criteria for dementia.

【28】With the increase in life expectancy over the past half century has come a huge increase in the numbers of patients with dementia. This is because in industrialized nations, greater than 90% of cases of dementia are due to AD, vascular disease, dementia with Lewy bodies/Parkinson's disease (DLB/PD), or some combination of all three, and the prevalence of these three disorders is strongly age-associated. Thus in the USA, the prevalence of all cases of dementia increases from less than 1% among those in their 60s to around 40% among patients over 90 years of age.

【29】Often the cause of dementia is obvious – e.g. as an aftermath of hypoxia or head trauma. Nonetheless, scores of diseases, toxins, or deficiencies can cause dementia , and many of these are fully reversible. Accordingly, each patient presenting with dementia deserves a thorough evaluation to rule out reversible etiologies. Although, in 2012, treatment options for most patients with dementia who have some combination of AD, vascular dementia, DLB/PD, or frontotemporal dementia remained disappointing, there is good reason to be optimistic than disease-modifying or even disease-preventing treatments will become available over the next few years.

【30】#### Clinical vignette

【31】An 81-year-old male was referred by his primary care doctor to a neurologist for visual hallucinations. His wife said that he reported seeing children without faces sitting down at the dining room table with him. The hallucinations occurred around the time the patient was eating dinner. When his wife said she didn't see them, he just got angry. The hallucinations started several months ago, each lasted several minutes, and occurred several times a week. No other alteration in consciousness was associated with these episodes.

【32】He had been an attorney who retired 6 years earlier. He had a history of hypertension, hyper-cholesterolemia, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, gastro-esophageal reflux disease, and benign prostatic hypertrophy. His medications included aspirin, tamsulosin, irbesartan, dronaderone, pantoprazole, and rosuvastatin. He had never smoked and stopped drinking alcohol because it exacerbated his atrial fibrillation.

【33】His wife said that at times he was as sharp as always, but at other times he was confused and out of it. He started taking a 2-hour nap every day. He had about a 20-year history of anosmia with no etiology found by an ENT.

【34】His wife said that he occasionally lost his balance and she was afraid he would fall. His gait had slowed. The patient and his wife agreed that his memory was about as good as that of others his age.

【35】He spent most of his day looking at TV. Occasionally he thought the people on TV were talking directly to him. He enjoyed going to Atlantic City and he reported playing poker as well as always.

【167】**HISTORY**

【168】**Congenital**

【169】The diagnosis is usually apparent from the history， although with spondylolisthesis， the symptoms， i.e. low lumbar backache， worse on standing， may not present until late childhood or early adult life.

【170】**Acquired**

【171】**_General_**

【172】The speed of onset is important. Sudden onset back pain may be due to trauma or disc lesions， whereas gradual onset of pain may be due to conditions such as degenerative disease. Mechanical lesions impinging on the cord can result in neurological symptoms such as bladder dysfunction (urinary retention). Symptoms worse on movement and relieved by rest suggest a mechanical cause，whereas pain that is severe and unrelenting can occur with malignant causes. In addition， there may be symptoms (other than musculoskeletal) related to the underlying cause such as abdominal pain， dysuria or menorrhagia.

【173】**_Traumatic_**

【174】There will usually be a clear history of trauma. Care must be taken in moving the patient. Neurological sequelae may be obvious.

【175】**_Infective_**

【176】There may be a history of TB； the patient may have had night sweats or cough. Osteomyelitis of the spine may also occur in diabetes and the immunocompromised， in which case the organism is more commonly Staphylococcus aureus. With spinal TB， the patient is usually young and complains of malaise， fever， pain， tenderness and limitation of movement of the spine. Discitis usually presents with mild backache accompanied by leg pain.

Ankylosing spondylitis usually affects young adult males. The sacroiliac joints are affected initially， then the whole spine. The|删除0换行|patient usually presents with lumbar stiffness， especially when rising in the morning. Iritis and plantar fasciitis may also occur.

【178】Rheumatology disorders may present with symptoms in other joints.

【179】_Neoplastic_

【180】The patient is usually unwell with severe unrelenting pain， often localised to a particular area of the spine. There may be a past history of a primary tumour (e.g. bronchus， breast， thyroid， prostate or kidney) or the primary may not be apparent. The pain may have been of sudden onset with a pathological fracture resulting in a collapsed vertebra. Rarely paraplegia may be a presenting symptom. Myeloma may present with backache.

【181】_Degenerative_

【182】Osteoarthritis usually presents in the older patient， with pain made worse on movement and relieved by rest. With intervertebral disc lesions， there is usually sudden onset of pain radiating down the back of the leg (sciatica). The pain is worse on movement， coughing and straining. Neurological symptoms may be present， e.g. weakness of a limb or bladder symptoms.

【183】**_Metabolic_**

【184】Osteoporosis is commonest in post-menopausal women.Osteoporosis itself does not cause pain but pathological fractures of the vertebra may occur， causing pain. Bone pain and pathological fractures occur. Osteomalacia may occur in adults with a history of gastrectomy， steatorrhoea， renal failure or anticonvulsant therapy.

【185】There may be a history of Cushing's disease or long-term steroid therapy. _Idiopathic_

【186】Paget's disease of bone may cause backache. This usually occurs over the age of 40 years. The patient may have noted other changes，e.g. enlargement of the face or bowing of the leg. Scheuermann’s disease is osteochondritis of the spine. It causes backache in adolescence. The patient may present because the parents have noticed round shoulders.

【187】This is very common. Check for malingering， anxiety， depression and compensation neurosis.

【188】**_Visceral_**

【189】With penetrating peptic ulcer， the patient complains of epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back. The pain may be relieved by food and antacids. With carcinoma of the pancreas， the patient will describe a boring pain in the back， which is unrelenting. There will be a history of anorexia and weight loss. The patient may be jaundiced. With carcinoma of the rectum， invasion of the sacrum and the sacral plexus may occur， causing low back pain with sciatica.

【190】**_Vascular_**

【191】Aortic aneurysm may cause back pain by eroding into the vertebral bodies. Alternatively， it may cause severe back pain due to rupture. The patient may have noticed a pulsation in the abdomen. Acute aortic dissection usually gives a severe tearing back pain associated with chest pain. The patient is usually shocked.

【192】**_Renal_**

【193】There is usually a dull， boring ache with carcinoma of the kidney. The patient may also complain of haematuria. With ureteric colic， the pain radiates from loin to groin and is severe， the patient being unable to get into a comfortable position. Inflammatory disease of the kidney presents with upper lumbar back pain. The patient may be feverish with rigors， and complain of frequency and dysuria.

【194】_Gynaecological_

【195】The pain is usually low back pain associated with pelvic discomfort. The patient may also complain of dysmenorrhoea， menorrhagia or post-menopausal bleeding.

【196】**EXAMINATION**

【197】Acute cord compression will cause bilateral leg pain with lower motor neurone signs at the level of the compression， and upper motor neurone signs below. Check for sphincter disturbance. Acute cauda equina compression causes root pain in the legs， saddle anaesthesia and disturbances of bladder and bowel function. In any patient with acute backache， the above signs should be sought and， if found，the appropriate urgent referral made to a neurosurgeon or spinal surgeon.

【198】**Congenital**

【199】Kyphoscoliosis and spina bifida are usually obvious on examination. With spondylolisthesis， a 'step' may be palpable in the line of the spinous processes， with a skin crease below. It usually involves L5slipping on S1， or， less commonly， L4 slipping on L5. Occasionally， there are neurological signs in the limbs.

【200】**_Traumatic_**

【201】This will usually be obvious. Careful positioning of the patient and full neurological examination should be carried out. Always check for associated injuries.

With acute osteomyelitis， there is pyrexia， malaise and local tenderness and spasm. With chronic osteomyelitis， e.g. due to TB，|删除0换行|there will be wasting of the paraspinal muscles， spasm and restricted movements. There may be a localised kyphosis or 'gibbus' due to vertebral collapse. A psoas abscess may be present in the groin.

【203】Paraplegia may occur. With discitis， there will be reduced movement of the spine.

【204】_Inflammatory_

【205】The patient with ankylosing spondylitis will present with a stiff spine. There will be flexion of the hips and spine. In the advanced case， the patient cannot raise the head to see in front. Check for iritis and plantar fasciitis. Rheumatological disease will also present with problems in other joints.

【206】_Neoplastic_

【207】With myeloma， in addition to backache， there may be pain in the ribs， long bones and skull. Bone tenderness will be present with secondary deposits. Palpate along the spine for tenderness. Check the chest， thyroid， breast， kidney and prostate for malignancy. Check for any neurological signs.

【208】_Degenerative_

【209】There will be limitation of movement of the spine with osteoarthritis. With acute disc lesion， there will be limitation of spine movement， lordosis and neurological symptoms of the lower limbs. Carry out a full neurological examination.

【210】**_Metabolic_**

【211】There may be evidence of recent vertebral collapse. Loss of height and curvature of the spine may eventually occur. With osteomalacia， apart from bone pain， there may be proximal myopathy， resulting in a waddling gait.

【212】**_Endocrine_**

【213】There may be signs of Cushing’s disease or prolonged steroid therapy， e.g. cushingoid facies， buffalo hump， proximal myopathy， abdominal striae， etc.

【214】_Idiopathic_

【215】In Paget's disease， check for changes in the skull and long bones (bowing of the tibia). Compressive symptoms due to skull enlargement may result in blindness， deafness or cranial nerve entrapment. There may be signs of high-output cardiac failure due to vascularity of bone. In Scheuermann's disease， there will be a smooth， thoracic kyphosis and， below this， a compensatory lumbar lor

【1】Commentary

【2】This patient presented with the classic triad of erythema, lymphadenopathy, and atypical cells in the blood. She also demonstrated other common findings, including hair loss and onychodystrophy. Because she had previously been partially treated, her flow cytometry did not formally meet criteria for a diagnosis of Sézary syndrome, with a CD4:CD8 ratio of only 6.9:1 and just 555/µL atypical cells. As a result of refractory disease despite multiple systemic treatments, she ultimately underwent a hematopoietic stem-cell transplant, the only definitive therapy available for this disease.

【3】Case 6.2

【4】A 62-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of diffuse pruritus refractory to treatment and a new peripheral eosinophilia. The itch had been intensifying over the last year and was accompanied by erythematous patches on her skin and the development of thickened, loose skin over her joints, back, abdomen, and thighs . Her axillae and groin were uninvolved, and she had no nail changes. She reported intermittent chills and fever for the last year.

【5】A peripheral blood smear revealed the presence of numerous lymphoid cells with cerebriform nuclei . A skin biopsy demonstrated a perivascular infiltrate of atypical CD4+ lymphoid cells  and a normal tissue elastin stain. Peripheral blood flow cytometry revealed a large population of atypical CD3+ cells, a CD4:CD8 ratio of 15:1, and loss of CD7 and CD26 on 85 % of T cells . The patient was diagnosed with Sézary syndrome.

【6】Although she underwent treatment with extracorporeal photophoresis, her condition continued to deteriorate. She developed severe onychodystrophy  and thickening and fissuring of the skin complicated by secondary infection .

【7】Commentary

【8】This patient presented with the classic triad of Sézary syndrome: erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and atypical cells in the blood (a CD4:8 ratio of 15:1 and loss of CD7 and CD26 on 85 % of cells). Her complete blood count also demonstrated a marked eosinophilia, a not uncommon finding in patients with Sézary syndrome. She was treated with extracorporeal photopheresis, a therapy that has shown significant success in treating (but not curing) Sézary syndrome. This case also highlights the point that patients with Sézary syndrome are at risk for frequent skin infections because of their immune-compromised state and damage to the skin, which in some cases can lead to sepsis and even death.

【61】7. Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma

【62】Keywords

【63】Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma ATLL HTLV-1 Acute Lymphomatous Chronic Smoldering Hypercalcemia Opportunistic infection Cerebriform cells Mycosis fungoides Sézary Flower cells Viral synapse Breastfeeding Proviral integration

【64】Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is an aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma caused by long-term infection with human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1). Patients with ATLL have an extremely poor prognosis, their disease complicated by multidrug resistance of malignant cells, infection due to impaired T-cell mediated immunity, hypercalcemia, and multiple organ failure. Half of patients develop cutaneous manifestations. The cutaneous lesions of ATLL are highly varied and include erythroderma, purpuric papules, and plaques. This chapter addresses the clinical presentation, prognosis, treatment, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular characteristics of this disease. It closes with a differential diagnosis and clinical case.

【65】7.1 Clinical
------------

【66】### 7.1.1 Clinical Presentation

【67】Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a rapidly progressive lymphoma of mature, peripheral, activated T lymphocytes, caused by HTLV-1 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 – 3 \]</u>. This lymphoma was first described in Japan in 1977 by Uchiyama et al. 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 4 \]</u>. ATLL occurs in adults at a median age of 55–58 years (range, 20–80 years) 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 3 \]</u>. There is a slight female predominance 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>.

【68】Both ATLL and its causative virus, HTLV-1, are endemic to southwestern Japan, the Caribbean, central Africa, and parts of South America 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 2 , 5 \]</u>. Around the world, an estimated 20 million people are infected with the virus 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 6 \]</u>. Approximately 2.5 % of those carriers of HTLV-1 will develop ATLL 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 2 \]</u>. Risk of transformation may be higher in men than in women 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 6 \]</u>. ATLL has a long latency period, and affected patients were likely infected at a very young age via breastfeeding or exposure to blood products, or later, via sexual transmission 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 2 \]</u>. HTLV-1 is a deltaretrovirus; infected cells demonstrate integration of proviral DNA into host cell genomes, which is likely responsible for the oncogenic nature of the virus 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 7 \]</u>.

【69】There are four variants of ATLL: acute, lymphomatous, chronic, and smoldering 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 8 \]</u>. Skin lesions develop in 43–72 % of patients with ATLL. Cutaneous manifestations of ATLL include papules or nodules that are erythematous or violaceous and occasionally ulcerated, scaly patches and plagues and rarely, erythroderma  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 4 , 9 – 11 \]</u>. Discrete cutaneous lesions are most common in the acute and lymphomatous variants; erythroderma is more common in chronic or smoldering ATLL 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>.

【44】**Diagnosis**

【45】**Diagnosis is low lumbar central developmental spinal stenosis. This is frequently caused by hypertrophy of the zygopophyseal joint capsules or osteophytosis. Usually there is a predisposing factor in the form of a trefoil spinal canal or otherwise congenitally narrow spinal canal. It could be multisegmental bilateral lateral stenosis but the chances of it affecting two levels bilaterally and equally are fairly remote. In any event， it makes no real difference， the treatment will be the same.**

【46】**Treatment**

**Because this condition is due to structural changes， treatment is really man-agement. The patient is instructed in things that he almost certainly already knows about daily activities—avoid extension postures that occur during|删除0换行|prolonged standing or overhead work， and extension activities such as fast walking. Flexion exercises can be helpful in reversing the symp-toms and mobilizing the spine over a very protracted period. Occasion-ally， lumbar traction increases the patient’s tolerance to extension and the patient can bc shown how to do this at home by lying supine， put-ting his calves on a chair， and contracting the hamstrings. This produces some minor lumbar traction， which can sometimes have a therapeutic effect out of all proportions to the mechanical effect. In addition， some patients receive long-lasting relief (a few wecks or months) with me-chanical lumbar traction applicd in flexion or neutral.**

【10】**5.11 The language variants of dementia and the acquired aphasia**

【11】**The description and explanation of acquired language disorders have a long-standing history and belong to the core of cognitive neuropsychology. The goal is to reconstruct the behavior of the patients by postulating processing modules and possible interactions between these modules， which have become selectively impaired by brain damage. With respect to the acquired language disorders， two well-known neurologists Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke were the first starting with this approach of localization of lan-guage functions based on specific impairment patterns. There are several reviews regarding the development of such explanatory models and Heilman(2006) published an excellent one， summarizing the progress focusing exclu-sively on the clinical data， that is， on patients with a vascular cause for their language deficit. Only a few years before this review was published， system-atic research on the different PPAs started. From a neuropathological view， there is a clear and outstanding difference between these two causes for aphasia： vascular lesions almost inevitably involve also white matter struc-tures and not only cortical areas. Thus vascular lesions concern the proces-sing modules and the connections between them. On the other hand， they are focal lesions. Neurodegenerative pathology primarily affects cortical neurons including their dendrites and axons and not independent white matter tracts. Although it may start in specific areas of the brain， at a stage in which a patient shows clinical impairment， many areas of the brain will already be involved， albeit with different intensity. Thus in some respect， they suffer from cortical lesions which are less focal than those after a stroke.**

【12】**In the beginning of this chapter we used a vascular schema to classify the aphasias into three different neurodegenerative variations. In the following para-graphs we will further discuss the similarities and differences between the vascu-lar and the neurodegenerative aphasias and base this discussion， for example， on the excellent paper from Mesulam， Thompson， Weintraub， and Rogalski (2015).**

【21】**Precedingly we focused on language production， let us now turn to the question of verbal comprehension. This is the domain in which the most obvious differences exist between acquired stroke-based and neurodegenera-tive causes for aphasia. If the source of the aphasia is a neurodegenerative process， the clinical syndrome is termed SD. After a stroke， the aphasia is referred to as Wernicke’s aphasia. Patients suffering from either SD or Wernicke's aphasia differ in the following aspects：**

【22】**Wernicke's aphasics do not understand sentences and words， whereas SD patients do not understand words 删除2:<u>(but seem to understand sentences)</u>.**

【23】** Patients with SD are typically not impaired in repetition of words and sentences， whereas patients with Wernicke’s aphasics are impaired in this respect.**

【24】** Wernicke's aphasics show severe patterns of paragrammatism and jargon， whereas SD patients produce semantic paraphasia but rarely jargon.**

【25】**SD patients often try to correct themselves or search for the correct word， whereas Wernicke’s aphasics have no insight in their language problems.**

【26】**Early in the disease， the comprehension deficit of the SD patients com-prises only infrequent and low imageable words. In this stage， wrong but semantically related words may become activated， therefore SD patients produce primarily semantic paraphasia. Later on， however， the specific instances of categories are also involved. This leads to an increasing usage of global and descriptive words (instead of goose → animal， etc.). If the understanding of some (an increasing number of) single words is impaired， hearing the context of the words， that is， the sentences they are embedded in， is helpful because the interpretation of single words is easier when more information is present. Therefore understanding sentences is less impaired in SD patients compared to understanding words. Moreover being able to understand on a phonological level and noticing that the to-be-conveyed message cannot be understood on this level will lead to correcting attempts. These correction attempts can be observed in SD but not in Wernicke's patients.**

Intending to speak and suffering from problems in processing the phonological word form on the conceptual level and at the same time in accessing the phono-logical word form may be called a“two-way” word-finding deficit： input and output from the conceptual level is impaired. 【43】**Acute polyarthritis (≤6 weeks) may be infective or non-infective. 【64】**1\. Is Pain Mechanical or Inflammatory?**

【65】**Mechanical pain-OA. Pain worse on movement or weight-bearing， relieved by rest， with minimal morning stiffness (<15 min) suggests OA. 【66】**· Idiopathic OA： Usually an elderly patient with longstanding symmetrical mechan-ical joint pain， commonly in knee (Asians)， hip (Caucasians)， spine or hands. 【67】**Secondary OA： Prior joint damage (e.g.， trauma， other inflammatory arthritis， gout， septic arthritis) increases the risk of OA. Secondary OA may present younger and more atypically than idiopathic OA.**

【68】**Inflammatory pain， on the other hand， is worse at rest， relieved by motion and associ-ated with prolonged morning stiffness (often 30 min or more). This is more typical of RA， SpA， gout and other rheumatologic disease.**

【102】·Lupus erythematosus is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease that affects the connective tissue and vasculature of various organs

【104】Classic discoid lesions of cutaneous lupus erythematosus appear as mildly scaling， erythematous， edematous， sharply demarcated plaques measuring up to 15 cm， involving scalp， face， upper trunk， and upper extremities； follicular plugging may be seen

【105】Older lesions appear atrophic with variable pigmentation

【106】Tumid form of lupus presents as indurated plaques and nodules without overlying erythema or atrophy

【112】IInterstitial deposits of mucin are noted in many cases

【113】Epidermal hyperplasia with papillomatosis is seen in the verrucous form of lupus

【114】In the dermal form of lupus erythematosus known as _tumid lupus erythematosus， there is superficial and_ deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate with interstitial mucin but no epidermal changes

【115】In lupus panniculitis， there is a lobular lymphocytic panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis and interstitial mucin， with or without epidermal changes

【126】The cardiovascular system consists of the heart， capillaries， veins， and lymphatics and functions in coordination with the pulmonary system to circulate oxygenated blood through the arterial system to all cells. 【115】**Case Study Analysis**

【116】After assessing the patient and obtaining a detailed history， the advanced practice provider(APP) found the patient to be experiencing mild anxiety as per the Patient Health Ques-tionnaire-9\* assessment tool. EKG showed a sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventric-ular contractions (PVCs)， which the patient described as the feeling he normally had when he felt dizzy and nauseated. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were 1.8 uIU/mL and fasting glucose was 80 mg/dL. These test results are considered normal.

【117】**_Diagnosis： Anxiety related to arrhythmia due to excessive caffeine ingestion_**

【118】From this assessment， the APP and patient discussed cutting back on caffeine intake from coffee and energy drinks and incorporating stress-reduction techniques. Patient felt these were reasonable changes and follow-up was set for 1 month later.

【119】Follow-up： At the 1-month follow-up the patient reported improvement of symptoms and only occasional anxiety related to work. EKG at this time demonstrated a normal sinus rhythm. Patient was counseled to return if symptoms recurred or if he began to feel over-whelmed or depressed.

【121】**INTRODUCTION TO COMPLAINT**

【122】· Hematuria can be visible (gross) or nonvisible (microscopic). Forty-five percent of all cases are attributable to infection (25%) and kidney stones (20%)

【123】· Urinary tract infections： invasion of bacteria via the urethra into the bladder

【124】· Urge to urinate， pain with urination， burning with urination

【125】·Foul smelling urine

【126】·Kidney infections： bacteria reach the kidneys via the ureters or via the bloodstream. Symptoms similar to urinary tract infection， often accompanied by fever and flank pain

【127】· Kidney stones： precipitation of minerals in the urine in the kidney forming stones； movement of stones often causes excruciating pain； can cause microscopic or gross hematuria

【128】·Kidney trauma： from a contact sport or other injury

【129】·Kidney disease： glomerulonephritis， primary or secondary to viral or strep infections

【130】· Ingested substances： ingestion of toxic substances can cause inflammation and damage to the filtration system of the kidney； cytoxan and penicillin can cause hematuria； ingestion of anticoagulants leads to hematuria， particularly if there is an underlying condition that causes the bladder to bleed

【131】·Inherited conditions： sickle cell anemia and Alport syndrome

【132】· Strenuous exercise： intense workouts can result in hematuria thought to be secondary to dehydration or breakdown of red blood cells (RBCs)， which occurs with sustained aerobic activity

【41】**_Lymphadenopathy_**

【42】A 73-year-old woman was referred to a physical therapy clinic by her oncologist with a diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy. She had a history of uterine cancer 20 years ago and a history of breast cancer 10 years ago.

Demonstrate all test maneuvers in order to prevent poor performance from a lack of under-standing rather than from neurologic impairment.

【102】Show the client the items you will be using and how they will be used. For light touch， dab the skin lightly； do not stroke.

【103】Tests are done with the client’s eyes closed. Ask the client to tell you where the sensation is felt or to identify “sharp”or“dull.” Apply the stimulus randomly and bilaterally over the face， neck， upper arms， hands， thighs，lowerlegs， and feet. Allow at least 2 seconds between the time the stimulus is applied and the next one is given. This avoids the summation effect.

【104】Follow-up with temperature using test tubes filled with hot and cold water and vibration using a low-pitch tuning fork over the peripheral joints. Temperature can be omitted if pain sensation is normal. Apply the stem of the vibrating tuning fork to the distal interphalangeal joint of the fingers and interphalangeal joint of the great toe， elbow， and wrist. Ask the client to tell you when vibration is first felt and when it stops. Remember， aging adults often lose vibratory sense in the great toe and ankle on both sides.

Again， all tests should be per-formed on both sides.

【1】 Rib fractures are more common in children younger than 1 year old, whereas diaphyseal injuries are more common in those older than 1 year old. This fact reflects the manner in which the child is typically held during the trauma.

【2】 Direct blows to the abdomen most frequently result in duodenal hematoma, pancreatitis (with its attendant complications), and hepatic and splenic injuries.

【3】 The diagnosis of nonaccidental trauma is established using a combination of history (i.e. incompatibility of the reported history in relation to the type and extent of injuries), physical findings (e.g. burns, hand marks, sexual abuse, preretinal hemorrhages), and radiographic findings.

【4】 A major diagnostic consideration is OI, in which a family history of fractures, deafness, blue sclerae, and poor dentition may be elicited. If necessary, the diagnosis can be confirmed with a skin biopsy demonstrating a collagen synthesis deficiency.

【5】 Another diagnostic consideration is Menkes’ syndrome, a very rare neurodegenerative disorder due to a defect in copper metabolism, leading to death within the first year of life. These patients have sparse, brittle hair, which accounts for the designation “kinky hair syndrome.”

【6】 Congenital rickets due to maternal vitamin D deficiency is a consideration in cases of suspected nonaccidental trauma, although there is still active debate over the degree of overlap in terms of clinical features between the two disease states.

【7】Radiologic

【8】 Child or infant abuse can have central nervous system, abdominal, or skeletal findings evident on imaging studies. The skeletal manifestations are reviewed below.

【9】 The CML is the most specific injury in child abuse. The CML is seen almost exclusively in children younger than 2 years old and most commonly seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, distal tibia and proximal humerus.

【10】 Depending on the radiographic projection, a CML may appear as a corner fracture or a so-called bucket handle fracture.

【11】 In addition to the CML, other injuries that are highly specific for child abuse include fractures in unusual locations such as the scapulae, sternum, and posterior ribs.

【12】 Injuries that are moderately specific for child abuse include fractures of varying ages, complex skull fractures, and fractures involving the digits or vertebral bodies.

【13】 Spiral fractures are injuries with low specificity for child abuse. However, suspicion should be raised when such fractures are seen in children who are not old enough to have engaged in activities that would make an accidental cause likely.

【14】 One spiral fracture that should not raise suspicion for child abuse is the “toddler’s fracture,” a spiral fracture of the distal tibia. This injury is seen in children who are learning to walk and is not an indication for performing a skeletal survey.

【15】 Physiologic periostitis in the infant is a normal bony condition, which is typically seen between 1 and 6 months of age. It is characteristically manifested as a single (or occasionally multiple) thin layer of periosteal reaction on the medial aspect of the femur, tibia, humerus, and radius, and is symmetric in distribution.

【16】 The radionuclide bone scan (and potentially whole-body MR imaging) is a complementary method to plain films for detection of injuries due to abuse. This imaging study is particularly sensitive for detection of posterior rib fractures as well as diaphyseal injuries (which may actually be bowing fractures that can be inapparent on plain films).

【29】DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

【30】 Congenital neuroblastoma: This entity typically has the radiologic appearance of a solid (rather than cystic) mass, whereas the lesions shown in the case presented here are hypoechoic (consistent with fluid). Although neuroblastoma could become cystic following chemotherapy or a biopsy producing internal hemorrhage, no history of these events is present in the patient shown here. Finally, neuroblastoma tends to distort the shape of the adrenal gland; however, in the case presented, the shape of the adrenal gland is preserved. For these reasons, neuroblastoma is an unlikely consideration.

【31】 Other retroperitoneal tumors (e.g. lymphangioma, teratoma): These tumors are very rarely located in the retroperitoneum. Furthermore, such lesions are usually calcified, fluid-filled masses. This diagnosis is an unlikely one.

【32】 Perinephric abscess: The mixed echogenicity seen in the case presented here could be seen in a phlegmon or abscess. However, no history of infection is present; furthermore, such a process would be very unusual in a newborn. Finally, a perinephric abscess would be expected to arise adjacent to, rather than within, the adrenal gland). However, in this case shown, the adrenal gland itself is the site of the abnormality. Perineph-ric abscess is an incorrect diagnosis.

【33】 Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: This entity might be considered because of the enlargement of the adrenal glands. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the glands do maintain their adreniform shape. However, enlargement of both glands is present, whereas, in the case shown here, a single adrenal gland is affected. Endo-crinologic abnormalities are helpful in supporting the diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. However, we are given no history of such abnormalities in the case presented here. Therefore, this diagnosis is unlikely.

【34】 Adrenal hemorrhage: In the case shown, the echotex-ture of the mass changed relatively quickly, which would be unusual for any entity other than hemorrhage. Furthermore, the shape of the adrenal gland is maintained, which would be unusual for some of the diagnostic considerations other than hemorrhage but common for adrenal hemorrhage. This diagnosis is correct.

【36】Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage

【37】KEY FACTS

【38】Clinical

【39】 Spontaneous adrenal hemorrhage occurs relatively commonly in newborn infants and is occasionally detected in utero.

【40】 Predisposing factors include perinatal stress, traumatic birth, hypoxia, and sepsis. Hemorrhage also occurs with increased frequency in large infants and infants of diabetic mothers.

【41】 Large hemorrhages can clinically present with systemic shock or a palpable mass; smaller hemorrhages cause mild anemia or jaundice. Biochemical abnormalities are seldom present in either the acute or convalescent phase.

【42】 Hemorrhage is more common in the left adrenal gland and is seen bilaterally in approximately 10% of cases.

【43】 Complications are uncommon but include renal vein thrombosis (especially when the left adrenal gland is involved) and secondary infection/abscess.

【44】Radiologic

【45】 The primary diagnostic considerations for a suprarenal mass in a neonate are acute adrenal hemorrhage and congenital neuroblastoma.

【46】 Doppler evaluation can help distinguish adrenal hemorrhage from neuroblastoma based on vascularity; a hematoma is typically avascular while a tumor is generally well vascularized.

【47】 At sonography, hemorrhage is typically initially echo-genic, next develops mixed echogenicity as the clot retracts, and becomes hypo- or anechoic as it liquefies.

【48】 Serial sonographic studies documenting rapidly decreasing size of the mass are consistent with adrenal hemorrhage. Progressive enlargement of the mass suggests a diagnosis of neuroblastoma and is an indication for surgical resection.

【49】 MR imaging has been used to establish the diagnosis but often does not definitively distinguish adrenal hemorrhage from neuroblastoma. Fortunately, small neu-roblastomas in the newborn invariably have favorable histology, which allows serial imaging with sonography without substantial risk of rapid growth.

【50】 Dystrophic calcifications can be the first radiologic indication of previous adrenal hemorrhage. Adrenal calcification, however, can also be seen in many other entities, such as neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, Wolman’s syndrome, pheochromocytoma, tuberculosis, and adrenal carcinoma.

【64】DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

【65】 Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN): The streaky hilar opacities and small amount of pleural fluid are consistent with TTN. The fact that the clinical and radiologic findings quickly resolved makes TTN the most likely diagnosis.

【66】 Respiratory distress due to surfactant deficiency (respiratory distress syndrome, hyaline membrane disease, surfactant deficiency disease): In respiratory distress syndrome, the lung volumes are typically reduced (except, on occasion, in infants who are intu-bated) and pleural fluid is very rarely present. The radiographic pattern is that of a diffuse, fine (so-called ground glass), granular appearance. These findings are all at variance with those depicted in the case presented here. Finally, respiratory distress syndrome is seen almost exclusively in preterm infants, whereas the patient in the case presented is a term infant. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【67】 Meconium aspiration: Generally, more patchy opacities (representing atelectasis) and focal air trapping are seen in meconium aspiration, rather than the streaky opacities seen in the case illustrated. Often, infants with meconium aspiration are quite ill, have persistent fetal circulation due to pulmonary hypertension, and are intubated—features that are not present in the case depicted here. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【68】 Congestive heart failure: In congestive heart failure, the heart size is typically enlarged, unlike the case shown here. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【69】 Neonatal pneumonia: This entity can initially have a radiographic appearance similar to the case shown here. However, the rapid resolution is not consistent with pneumonia. Furthermore, clinical information supporting infection (e.g. prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever, infant leukocytosis or leukope-nia, infected amniotic fluid) is not present in the case illustrated. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【70】DIAGNOSIS

【71】Transient tachypnea of the newborn (retained fetal lung fluid, wet-lung syndrome, persistent pulmonary edema)

【72】KEY FACTS

【73】Clinical

【74】 The physiologic abnormality underlying TTN is delayed clearance of normal fetal lung fluid from the pulmonary interstitium.

【75】 TTN is probably the most common cause of neonatal respiratory distress.

【76】 This entity is slightly more common in boys.

【77】 Risk factors for TTN include prolonged labor, delivery by cesarean section, precipitous delivery, maternal diabetes, neonatal hypoproteinemia, and maternal administration of hypotonic fluid.

【78】 In TTN, tachypnea is present within the first few hours of life. Respiratory distress peaks by 24 hours and is nearly always resolved by 2 to 3 days. Other clinical features include occasional grunting, sternal and intercostal retractions, and mild cyanosis.

【79】 Treatment is conservative and usually consists of placement of the infant under an oxygen hood. Antibiotics are sometimes administered if it is unclear whether infection is the cause of symptoms.

【80】 Neonatal pneumonia (primarily that due to infection by group B streptococcus, gram negative rods, or Listeria), hyaline membrane disease, meconium aspiration, asphyxia, congestive heart failure, and TTN can have similar clinical presentations in the first few hours of life.

【81】Radiologic

【82】 The radiographic appearance is typically that of streaky, coarse reticular opacities that have hazy borders. Well-defined focal opacities are rare.

【83】 Lung volumes are normal or increased in TTN, and the heart size is normal.

【84】 Radiographic improvement generally parallels clinical improvement.

【85】 Pulmonary effusions are usually small and are more common in the right hemithorax.

【86】 Follow-up radiographs are not necessary when the clinical and radiographic presentations are typical.

【98】DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

【99】 Hypoperfusion complex (also known as “shock bowel”): This entity is usually seen in the setting of posttraumatic hypovolemic shock and has the imaging findings of (1) abnormally increased contrast-enhancement of the pancreas, adrenal glands, kidneys, and bowel wall; (2) fluid-filled bowel loops with free peritoneal fluid; and (3) a small aorta and inferior vena cava (IVC) due to the reduced blood volume. In the case presented here, the IVC is relatively small but the aorta appears normal; no significant enhancement of the adrenals and pancreas is seen. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【100】 Uncomplicated hemoperitoneum: The case illustrated shows free intraperitoneal fluid that could be blood (or urine and bile, because these have a similar appearance). However, bowel wall contrast-enhancement is present, which would not be expected in uncomplicated hemoperitoneum. This diagnosis is unlikely.

【101】 Pancreatic trauma: Pancreatic fractures (which can be clinically undetected) may be associated with bowel dilatation secondary to local ileus. However, the resultant fluid collections would be expected to be retroperitoneal (unlike the case shown here). Furthermore, bowel wall contrast-enhancement would not be expected. This diagnosis is incorrect.

【102】 Bowel and mesenteric injury: Given the free intraperitoneal fluid, bowel wall contrast-enhancement and bowel dilatation in the presence of a normal caliber aorta and IVC, this diagnosis is reasonable and is the most likely.

【103】DIAGNOSIS

【104】Bowel perforation (without evidence of pneumoperitoneum)

【105】KEY FACTS

【106】Clinical

【107】 Substantial bowel and mesenteric trauma are found in 3% to 5% of children with blunt abdominal trauma.

【108】 The clinical signs of bowel injury are nonspecific, but include abdominal tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness, and absent bowel sounds.

【109】 Injuries of the bowel are associated with markedly increased morbidity and mortality; the decision to perform surgery is usually based on physical examination laboratory findings.

【110】Radiologic

【111】 The only definitive CT signs of bowel perforation are the presence of pneumoperitoneum and extravasated oral contrast material. Pneumoperitoneum occurs in 30% to 40% of patients with documented perforation but can be subtle. Extravasation of oral contrast material is rarely seen; thus, the decision to administer (or withhold) oral contrast material should not be based on the expectation of finding extravasated contrast material.

【112】 Typical CT findings include bowel wall thickening, contrast-enhancement, and otherwise unexplained peritoneal fluid.

【123】**CLINICAL DECISION MAKING Case Study Analysis**

【124】Based on the history of GERD， morning coughing， progressive dysfunction， and heartburn this was thought to be an esophageal stricture， which can be a complication of GERD due to repeated exposure to stomach acid， which causes changes to the esophageal lining. An upper endoscopy was performed， which showed inflammation and narrowing of the esoph-agus， confirming this diagnosis. A barium swallow was not performed as this would not show a cause for narrowing； motility testing was not used as this was not suspected to be a nerve problem， and labs were not needed as there was no evidence of bleeding.

【125】**_Diagnosis： Esophageal stricture related to long-term GERD_**

【126】Dilation was performed during the endoscopy and the patient was instructed to take 20mg omeprazole twice a day until follow-up at 1 month. The patient was also instructed to engage in mindful eating-to chew food thoroughly， not to rush during meals， and take frequent sips of water between bites of fo S1PS Ofod. Additionally， it was reinforced that the patient should remain in an upright position for at least 1 hour after eating， to avoid eating at least for 4 hours before going to sleep， and to sleep on several pillows to prevent reflux. Food and beverages to be avoided or taken in extremely limited quantities include chocolate， cola beverages， caffeine， highly spiced foods， and alcohol since these items are known to irri-gate gastric and esophageal mucosa. Depending upon the results ofthe 1-month follow-up examination， further interventions may be required.

They suggest that existing fMRI studies in healthy subjects show that affective empathy is related to the ante-rior insular and cingulate cortex in the case of negative emotions， to ventral striatum and the orbitofrontal cortex in the case of positive emotions. Cognitive empathy， on the other hand， relies on a temporal-frontal neuronal network including， for example， the temporoparietal junction and the cuneus删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Shdo et al.， 2018； Stietz et al.， 2019； Thiel， Studte， Hildebrandt， Huster， &Weerda， 2014)</u></u>， which are not primary sites for atrophy in bvFTD. The model of Seeley (2008) postulates that the disease starts in the anterior right insular and cingulate cortex， and these brain areas are related to the discrimination of(negative) emotions 删除1:<u>(Stietz et al.， 2019)</u>. In this respect， the two meta-analytic review of Bora et al. (2016) and Henry et al. (2014) lend the model of Seeley strong plausibility， because the first one argues that bvFTD patients do not suf-fer from a deficit of recognizing emotions globally， but only of that emotions which are related to the integrity of the insular cortex. The second one shows that bvFTD patients are definitely impaired in affective empathy， whereas the impairment in cognitive empathy might be derived from executive functions deficits， which covary with cognitive empathy.

【1】However， as mentioned earlier， the study of Roca et al. (2013) also dem-onstrated deficits in cognitive discounting in patients with early bvFTD (not only in affective empathy). Problems in discounting impulsive choice or in shifting preferences have been documented often in patients in an early stage of bvFTD 删除1:<u>(Manes et al.， 2011)</u>. In any case， they are present in the later phase of the disease. However， their presence in early bvFTD patients has not always been replicated 删除1:<u>(Kloeters， Bertoux， O'Callaghan， Hodges， &Hornberger， 2013)</u>. Moreover the possibility to discriminate bvFTD patients from AD patients using discounting tests like the IOWA gambling task and reversal learning seems to lower than that of emotion recognition， that is， tests for affective empathy 删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Bertoux et al.， 2013； Torralva et al.， 2009； Torralva et al.， 2015)</u></u>.

【2】**Consequently， BvFTD seem to start with impairment in affective empa-thy； however not necessarily with theory of mind problems and problems of discounting or reversal learning. As these latter impairments are also part of the clinical syndrome， however， their presence is more variable in the early phase of the disease. And they may be related to executive functioning impairments， which can be assessed with more traditional neuropsychologi-cal tests. The existing neuropsychological findings therefore endorse the model of Seeley (2008)， at least up to now.**

【13】#### Introduction

【14】The term headache applies to pain involving the head or facial structures . The characteristics of the pain and the pattern of associated symptoms vary with the headache type and the nature of any underlying pathology. In any given year, more than 90% of the population experiences at least one headache . The causes of headache range from short-lived, monophasic conditions such as viral infections or minor head injury, to intermittent and quality-of-life-threatening disorders such as migraine, to devastating and life-threatening disorders such as subarachnoid hemorrhage headache. A simplified approach to categorizing the many causes of headache is presented in Table 30.1 which follows the International Classification of Headache Disorders , second edition (ICHD-2) and identifies three major groups: primary and secondary headache disorders, and cranial neuralgias.

【19】The diversity of causes and the high prevalence of headaches make a systematic approach to diagnosis essential. Anatomically, head or facial pain can occur with any process that results in stimulation of the afferent branches of the trigeminal nerve and the sensory branches of other cranial or upper cervical nerves. In addition to pain of peripheral origin, headaches may arise within the central nervous system.

【20】In this chapter, we present a three-step approach to headache diagnosis. The first step is to identify or exclude secondary headache disorders by history, physical examination and judicious use of diagnostic tests . Second, we consider four syndromic groups of primary headache disorders, based on headache frequency and duration . Finally, we emphasize the identification of specific disorders within syndromic groups.

【31】#### Identifying or excluding secondary headache

【32】Secondary headaches are attributable to underlying organic or psychiatric disorders . In contrast, for primary headaches the headache disorder, such as migraine or tension type headache, is the problem. Secondary headaches should be suspected if “red flags” are present. Table 30.2 summarizes common red flags, the diagnoses they suggest, and a work-up to be considered. In addition to red flags, it is helpful to search for comfort signs. Comfort signs suggest that a primary headache disorder is likely. These include a long duration of similar headaches, menstrual exacerbation, a positive family history of similar headaches, and a typical response to treatment.

【33】通用删除16(英):<u>Figure 30.1 Headache diagnosis.</u>

【34】In a patient with red flags, diagnostic tests are usually required to identify or exclude the secondary headache disorder. In the process of differential diagnosis, it is imperative to realize that one patient may have more than one headache type. It should also be remembered that a patient who has a long history of a primary headache disorder may have a significant change in frequency, severity, or associated symptoms. This and other red flags should alert the physician to the possibility of new secondary headache disorder. The first step in the differential diagnosis of headache is therefore identifying or excluding a secondary headache disorder.

【35】#### Diagnosing a specific headache syndrome

【36】After excluding a secondary headache disorder, the next step is to identify a primary headache syndrome. Common headache syndromes and the specific disorders to consider within each syndromic group are summarized in Table 30.3 . These syndromes are defined based on the number of headache days per month and on the average duration of attacks. Based on headache days, there are two broad categories: chronic daily headache with 15 or more days per month and episodic headache with fewer than 15 headache days per month. Based on duration, we consider short duration attacks to be those lasting less than 4 hours on average and long duration attacks those which last 4 hours or more.

【37】The most common syndromic group are the episodic headaches of long duration; this group includes both episodic migraine and episodic tension type headache. The chronic daily headache of the long duration group includes four disorders: chronic migraine, chronic tension type headache, new daily persistent headache, and hemicrania continua. For the two groups characterized by headaches of short duration, the most important disorders are the trigeminal autonomic cephalgias, including cluster headache.

【38】Many ICHD-2 defined disorders are included in more than one syndromic group. Having identified the syndrome the next task is to diagnose the specific disorder in the syndromic group. In the sections that follow, we discuss a number of specific primary headache disorders .

【39】#### Primary headache disorder: migraine

【40】Migraine is the most disabling of the primary headache disorders, affecting about 12% of the US population. Migraine without aura is the most common form; diagnostic criteria are presented in Table 30.4 . In approximately 20–25% of migraine patients, however, the headache may be preceded by an aura. Auras are focal neurologic symptoms that are most commonly visual. Aura features are typically both positive (flashing lights, zig-zag lines) and negative (a graying out of vision). This differentiates aura from other causes of transient neurologic deficits including epilepsy, which is characterized by positive features, and stroke, which is characterized by negative features. Auras typically last between 5 and 60 minutes. These symptoms are fully reversible. Other common aura symptoms could include sensory symptoms or dysphasic speech (also fully reversible). These can occur simultaneously or in succession. Headache may begin during the aura or within 60 minutes of its resolution. More common than aura are premonitory symptoms which occur in about 60% of people with migraine. Premonitory features begin hours or days prior to headache and include fatigue, neck discomfort, yawning, food cravings, irritability, restlessness, euphoria, drowsiness, fluid retention, polyuria, diarrhea, constipation, photophobia, phonophobia, and osmophobia in various combinations.
